clue.text: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite

definitions.text: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite

parts.words: Heroine portrayed as a lady, or toxophilite
parts.note: Henry James's The Portrait of a Lady centres on a heroine surnamed Archer, and a toxophilite is an archer, so both halves point at her

explanation.surface: A heroine painted as a lady, or perhaps as a bowman.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Portrayed as a lady' points to Henry James's novel The Portrait of a Lady; the heroine's surname, Archer, is what 'toxophilite' (a lover of archery) means.
explanation.definitionFit: The heroine of James's novel is Miss Archer by surname, so the clue's two hints both name her.

clue.text: Composer in abandoned shop, right at end

indicators.note: abandoned behaviour is wild and unrestrained, so the letters of shop are thrown into a new order

explanation.surface: A composer found in a deserted shop with the right-hand side at the end.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abandoned' rearranges SHOP to SPOH, and 'right at end' adds R last.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Spohr was a German Romantic composer and violinist.

clue.text: Patient and courageous little woman

parts.note: points to the gentle, brave sister in Louisa May Alcott's Little Women, who falls ill and dies

explanation.surface: Praise for a brave, uncomplaining small lady.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Little woman' is the title of Alcott's Little Women, not a remark on height; the patient and courageous sister is the third March girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Beth is the quiet, self-sacrificing March sister in Alcott's novel of the four sisters.

clue.text: Small character from Steinbeck? Hardly

parts.note: the giant simple-minded farmhand in Of Mice and Men has the surname Small, though he is enormous

explanation.surface: Was there a minor figure in Steinbeck? Not really.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Small' is a surname, not a size: the character in Of Mice and Men is called Small, yet he is a huge man, hence 'Hardly'.
explanation.definitionFit: The big, gentle companion of George Milton in Of Mice and Men bears the surname Small.

clue.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

definitions.text: Agnes, who went far with Forster

parts.words: Agnes, who went far with Forster
parts.note: Agnes is a character in E. M. Forster's The Longest Journey, so 'went far' stands for that title

explanation.surface: A woman named Agnes who travelled a long way alongside a novelist.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Went far' refers to the title of Forster's novel The Longest Journey, in which Agnes is the hero's wife; her maiden surname is the answer, also a Cambridge college and a Welsh town.
explanation.definitionFit: Agnes, wife of Rickie in Forster's The Longest Journey, has this surname before her marriage.

clue.text: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque

definitions.text: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque

parts.words: Persistently profligate, puncturing pride, personification of the picaresque
parts.note: describes Tobias Smollett's dissolute hero of a 1751 picaresque novel, in a string of words that all start with the letter that begins both his names

explanation.surface: A run of alliterative praise for a wayward rogue of the road novel.
explanation.walkthrough: The alliteration on P is the hint: the hero of Smollett's picaresque novel has a first name and surname that both start with P.
explanation.definitionFit: Smollett's 1751 novel follows a wayward, prankish young rake through a picaresque series of adventures.

clue.text: Chaps surround fool and French composer

indicators.note: the chaps go round the outside of the fool, enclosing that word

parts.note: chaps are men
an ass is a fool
et is the French word for and

explanation.surface: Some fellows gather round a clown together with a French composer.
explanation.walkthrough: 'French' looks like part of the definition, since the composer is French, but it pairs with 'and' to give the French word for and; 'surround' puts the fool inside the chaps.
explanation.definitionFit: Jules Massenet was the French composer of the operas Manon and Werther.

clue.text: Ardent youth has computer memory, ex officio

parts.note: ROM is read-only memory in a computer
e.o. is the standard abbreviation for ex officio

explanation.surface: A keen young man has a computer's memory, by virtue of his office.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's passionate young lover gives his name to any amorous young man.

clue.text: Account of love game in Indian doubles match

definitions.text: Account of love game in Indian doubles match

parts.words: Account of love game in Indian doubles match
parts.note: reads like a tennis report of a game to love in a doubles match in India, but describes the ancient Indian treatise on lovemaking between couples

explanation.surface: A sports report of a love game in a doubles match played in India.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Love game' and 'doubles match' are tennis terms on the surface; here they mean lovemaking and pairing, in an Indian text.
explanation.definitionFit: The Sanskrit treatise attributed to Vatsyayana is a guide to erotic love between couples.

clue.text: King of Norway may be a first-born

indicators.note: the letters of the phrase may be rearranged into another word, so they are reshuffled

explanation.surface: A Norwegian king might well be an eldest son.
explanation.walkthrough: 'May be' rearranges the ten letters of A FIRST-BORN.
explanation.definitionFit: In Hamlet the young prince of Norway takes the Danish throne at the end and rules Norway's forces.

clue.text: Notes of Bohemian girl

parts.note: mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale, and the plural asks for it twice
mi is the third note of the sol-fa scale, and the plural asks for it twice

explanation.surface: Musical notes belonging to a girl from Bohemia.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bohemian' points to Puccini's La Bohème, whose heroine is the seamstress; it also recalls Balfe's opera The Bohemian Girl.
explanation.definitionFit: Puccini's consumptive seamstress in La Bohème lives among the Parisian artists of the Latin Quarter.

clue.text: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded

definitions.text: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded

parts.words: Super way W. H. Davies proceeded
parts.note: W. H. Davies wrote The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp, so his super way of getting about was on foot as a vagrant

explanation.surface: The excellent manner in which the poet Davies travelled.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Super' looks like praise, but it completes Davies's title The Autobiography of a Super-Tramp, about his years as a vagrant walking the roads.
explanation.definitionFit: Davies spent years roaming Britain and America as a vagrant, walking from place to place.

clue.text: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time

definitions.text: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time

parts.words: Constantia Durham and Clara Middleton identified one in time
parts.note: the two women engaged to Sir Willoughby Patterne in Meredith's novel each saw his self-centredness before marrying him

explanation.surface: Two Victorian women recognised a certain kind of man before it was too late.
explanation.walkthrough: Both women break off engagements to Sir Willoughby in George Meredith's 1879 novel, which takes its title from his vice.
explanation.definitionFit: Meredith's novel names its self-absorbed hero by his defining trait, the one both fiancées detect.

clue.text: Spring incitement, like fame

parts.note: Milton's Lycidas says fame is the goad that ... the clear spirit on, so this incitement springs a rider's horse forward

explanation.surface: Something that inspires in springtime, rather like renown.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Like fame' quotes Milton's Lycidas: 'Fame is the spur that the clear spirit doth raise'. 'Spring' is a verb's sense here, urging forward, not the season.
explanation.definitionFit: A rider's goad, and by extension any stimulus to action, is what Milton called fame.

clue.text: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)?

definitions.text: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)?

parts.words: Like Margaret Oliphant's curate not preferred (though later seen in charge)
parts.note: Oliphant's Chronicles of Carlingford include a novel about a curate who stays unpromoted, a title also given to a clergyman in permanent charge of a parish

explanation.surface: A Victorian novelist's curate passed over for promotion, though in charge later on.
explanation.walkthrough: Oliphant's novel The Perpetual Curate (1864) follows Frank Wentworth; the adjective seems to say he is never preferred, though a perpetual curate was in fact in charge of a parish.
explanation.definitionFit: The title adjective means unending, as of a curate who never rises higher.

clue.text: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)

definitions.text: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)

parts.words: "A poet is the most unpoetical thing in existence, because he has no — " (Keats)
parts.note: a gap-fill from Keats's 1818 letter to Richard Woodhouse on the chameleon poet, who lacks a fixed self

explanation.surface: A quotation from Keats about poets lacking a certain quality.
explanation.walkthrough: The line comes from Keats's letter of 27 October 1818 describing the poet as a chameleon with no self of his own.
explanation.definitionFit: Keats argued the poet has no fixed self or character, constantly filling some other body.

clue.text: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this

definitions.text: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this

parts.words: All Virginia Woolf's homes should have been at least this
parts.note: Woolf argued in A Room of One's Own that a woman writer needs a private space, so a home needs one for her and another for everyone else

explanation.surface: A remark on the minimum size of the novelist's houses.
explanation.walkthrough: Woolf's essay A Room of One's Own insists a woman needs a room to herself to write; a household then needs that room plus at least one more.
explanation.definitionFit: A house with a pair of chambers allows one private space for the writer and one shared.

clue.text: Gudrun and Ursula were in love

definitions.text: Gudrun and Ursula were in love

parts.words: Gudrun and Ursula were in love
parts.note: the two sisters of D. H. Lawrence's Women in Love, and The Rainbow before it, share a family surname

explanation.surface: Two women were both smitten.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In love' is the title Women in Love, in which Gudrun and Ursula are sisters; the clue asks their surname.
explanation.definitionFit: Lawrence's sisters Gudrun and Ursula belong to the Nottinghamshire family at the heart of The Rainbow and Women in Love.

clue.text: Reran the new version for devout poet

indicators.note: a new version of the words gives their letters in a fresh order

explanation.surface: Someone replayed the latest edition for a religious poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'New version' rearranges the eight letters of RERAN THE.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Traherne was a seventeenth-century English clergyman and mystical religious poet.

clue.text: Nothing to spoil mathematician-poet

parts.note: O, the figure zero, means nothing
to mar something is to spoil it

explanation.surface: Nothing can spoil the work of a scholar who wrote verse.
explanation.definitionFit: Omar Khayyam was a Persian mathematician and astronomer, famed for the Rubaiyat quatrains.

clue.text: Keneally's young surgeon seen in chapel hampered by scepticism

indicators.note: the name can be seen inside the run of letters of the next words

explanation.surface: An Australian novelist's young doctor, spotted in a church, held back by doubt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seen in' marks the letters inside chaPEL HAMpered; 'by scepticism' only completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Thomas Keneally's novel about early convict Australia features a young surgeon of this name.

clue.text: Composer in danger, manfully opposed

indicators.note: the name sits in the letters of the following words, across the comma

explanation.surface: A composer in peril, bravely resisting.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In' marks the letters inside danGER, MANfully; 'opposed' only completes the surface.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Edward German was an English composer of light opera, such as Merrie England.

clue.text: Donald Farfrae (as city father) sounds like horse's mother

indicators.note: spoken aloud, the word for the horse's parent matches the title

parts.note: a female horse is a mare

explanation.surface: A Hardy character in civic office resembles a female horse.
explanation.walkthrough: In Hardy's The Mayor of Casterbridge, Donald Farfrae, a Scot, eventually takes the civic office Henchard once held.
explanation.definitionFit: A city father is the head of a town council, the post Farfrae wins in Hardy's novel.

clue.text: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters

definitions.text: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters

parts.words: Suitable setting for spine-chiller by Minette Walters
parts.note: Minette Walters's first crime novel (1992) is named after a cold storage building, a fitting place for a chilling story

explanation.surface: A fitting location for a frightening crime novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spine-chiller' plays on cold: Walters's debut thriller is The Ice House, and an outbuilding for storing frozen blocks is a chilly setting.
explanation.definitionFit: Walters's debut novel takes its title from the old cold-store building where a body is found.

clue.text: Sister of 25 from Lewis

parts.note: refers to the Pevensie children in C. S. Lewis's Narnia books, the elder girl being the youngest's sister

explanation.surface: A sibling of another clue's answer, from the Hebridean island.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewis looks like the Hebridean island but is C. S. Lewis; the Pevensie sisters of the Narnia books are the elder and the youngest of four.
explanation.definitionFit: In The Lion, the Witch and the Wardrobe the elder Pevensie girl is the youngest child's sister.

clue.text: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy

definitions.text: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy

parts.words: One of those with whom Macheath could have been happy
parts.note: Macheath in Gay's The Beggar's Opera sings 'How happy could I be with either, were t'other dear charmer away', of Polly Peachum and the jailer's daughter

explanation.surface: One of a highwayman's possible happy partners.
explanation.walkthrough: In John Gay's The Beggar's Opera (1728) Macheath is torn between Polly Peachum and Lockit's daughter, the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Lockit's daughter is one of the two women Macheath sings he could be happy with.

clue.text: Why mistake different Winchester boy?

indicators.note: a different arrangement of the words gives another spelling, so the letters move around

explanation.surface: Why mistake a different boy from the school?
explanation.walkthrough: 'Different' rearranges the ten letters of WHY MISTAKE. Winchester College is an old English public school founded by William of Wykeham.
explanation.definitionFit: A pupil of Winchester College is named after its founder, William of Wykeham.

clue.text: She supervised What Katy Did at School

definitions.text: She supervised What Katy Did at School

parts.words: She supervised What Katy Did at School
parts.note: in Susan Coolidge's 1873 sequel the school at Hillsover is run by a tall, strict principal, whose surname is also an Italian city

explanation.surface: A woman oversaw the doings of a schoolgirl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'What Katy Did at School' reads as an account of a girl's conduct, but it is Susan Coolidge's book title; the strict head of the school in it is Mrs Florence.
explanation.definitionFit: The principal of Katy's boarding school in Coolidge's novel bears this surname, shared with the Tuscan city.

clue.text: Ancient quarter in holy city

definitions.meaning: the old walled native quarter of a North African town is called by this Arabic name
Islam's second holiest city, in Saudi Arabia, where Muhammad is buried

explanation.surface: An old district in a sacred city.
explanation.definitionFit: The Arabic word for town names both the old walled district of North African cities and the Saudi city of the Prophet's tomb.
